$comment: Pinned non-match/non-informational classifications for the PDO differential matrix (M1 design §2.9). Entries may only be REMOVED (a gap filled) or have their class changed by a deliberate edit reviewed alongside the code change. Adding an entry documents a limitation and requires `why` (>= 40 chars) to explain WHY it currently refuses/differs and, where applicable, what a customer should do instead. Populated from a real conformance run (check 28) against cloudflare/worker/fixtures/counter/app/Probe.php on php-wasm PHP 8.3.32 — see cloudflare/worker/scripts/gen-pdo-matrix.mjs (a later step) for how this becomes cloudflare/docs/pdo-compatibility.md.

bind.execute_array.types.why: execute([42, 42]) binds the array elements with their NATIVE PHP types on our side (int 42 stays INTEGER); real pdo_sqlite stringifies EVERY value passed to execute() regardless of its PHP type (measured — design §3 F-12). This is a DELIBERATE, PERMANENT pinned deviation, not a gap: matching real's stringify-everything behaviour would push wide integers through as TEXT literals and defeat inlineWideIntegers()'s int64 exactness. Use bindValue() with an explicit type when you need PDO's stringification.

bind.execute_empty_array_keeps_bound.why: execute([]) is treated as an explicit (empty) replacement of any bound values, so the placeholder is left unsupplied. Design §3 F-13 proposed the OPPOSITE fix (reuse bound values) from an 8.4-desktop measurement, but measured IN-GUEST — against this build's own real pdo_sqlite, the referee this milestone uses — execute([]) does NOT reuse a bound value either (it answers the unbound placeholder as NULL, its own SQLite default); the desktop measurement does not hold here. What differs is what workerd does with the resulting placeholder-count mismatch: ctx.storage.sql.exec() throws (sql_error) when given fewer bindings than '?' marks, where real SQLite's C API silently binds NULL for an unsupplied parameter. This is the SAME failure family as bind.named.missing (design §3 F-33): SQLite's own silent-NULL leniency here is a silent-wrong-answer risk, so refusing is not merely unfilled — pass execute(null) (no arguments) to keep bound values, which does match.

bind.mixed_named_and_positional.why: A statement binding both a named (:k) and a positional (?) placeholder throws SQLSTATE[HY093] on our side: NamedParams::rewrite() treats a bindings array containing ANY non-int key as entirely named, so the sole ? is never resolved and its bound value is reported as an unused named binding. Real pdo_sqlite executes this via SQLite's own shared ordinal sequence (named and positional placeholders share one ordinal, left to right in the SQL text) and answers a row. Orchestrator decision (M1 review round 2, R7): implementing that ordinal model is out of scope for this milestone; bind every placeholder in a statement the SAME way (all positional, or all named) to avoid this refusal.

bind.named.extra.why: An extra, unused named binding throws on both sides, but with different SQLSTATEs: ours reports HY093 ("not present in the statement") at rewrite time, real reports HY000 ("column index out of range", measured) at bind time. Both refuse the ambiguous input; only the SQLSTATE differs.

bind.named.missing.why: A missing named binding throws SQLSTATE[HY093] on our side; real SQLite silently binds the unsupplied parameter to NULL without complaining (measured — design §3 F-33). This is a DELIBERATE strictness, not merely a gap: SQLite's silent-NULL behaviour here is itself the kind of silent-wrong-answer failure mode this milestone exists to eliminate, so ours refuses loudly instead of guessing NULL was intended.

bind.named.reuse.why: execute([':a' => 5]) binds the same named placeholder used twice; real pdo_sqlite stringifies the value via execute()'s array path (the same stringify-everything behaviour as bind.execute_array.types / design §3 F-12), giving TEXT '5' at both positions, while ours preserves the native PHP int 5. Same permanent, pinned root cause as bind.execute_array.types — bindValue() with an explicit type sidesteps it.

bind.value.param_lob.why: bindValue($p, $v, PARAM_LOB) throws unconditionally today; binary values do not cross the JSON bridge, so this is refused rather than silently mangled. Real pdo_sqlite accepts it and stores it as a normal string. Store the value base64-encoded as text instead.

bind.value.position_zero.why: bindValue(0, ...) throws a \ValueError on both sides ('must be greater than or equal to 1') — SQLite/PDO positions are 1-based, and this shim now validates the same range real PDO does (M1 review round 2, R3) rather than silently accepting a bogus position that would only surface as a confusing failure later.

bind.value.wide_int_min.why: M1 review F-11: the NEGATIVE end of the wide-int band was previously unexercised. Binding PHP_INT_MIN and reading it straight back (no CAST) hits the SAME int64_precision wall as bind.value.wide_int_param_int, just on the negative side of zero (mvp-spec.md Appendix item 1): workerd's SQL->JS conversion loses precision for any value in the ambiguous magnitude band regardless of sign. Bind the wide integer as a string instead (see bind.value.wide_int_param_str, which matches) and CAST(... AS TEXT) when reading it back.

bind.value.wide_int_param_int.why: Binding PHP_INT_MAX and reading it straight back (no CAST) hits the same int64_precision wall a stored wide integer does (mvp-spec.md Appendix item 1): workerd's SQL->JS conversion loses precision for any value in the ambiguous band regardless of how it entered SQLite. Bind the wide integer as a string instead (see bind.value.wide_int_param_str, which matches) and CAST(... AS TEXT) when reading it back.

dup.both.why: FETCH_BOTH over duplicate column names needs the full 4-value arity; Branch A's `columns` list (cursor.columnNames, design §2.7) lets us DETECT the duplicate precisely now, so instead of silently answering with the wrong arity (the pre-fill deviation) we refuse loudly — real pdo_sqlite answers with the true 6-entry BOTH shape (measured), which the wire's last-wins `{column: value}` collapse has already made unrecoverable on our side. Alias duplicate columns distinctly (see dup.aliased, which matches) rather than relying on FETCH_BOTH over ambiguous column names.

dup.bound_by_index.why: FETCH_BOUND reads a bound column's value from the row positionally, by the 0-based index bindColumn() resolved against the true (duplicate-preserving) column list; once a duplicate name has collapsed two columns into one wire entry, that index no longer lines up with the collapsed row (M1 review round 2, R1). Measured: real pdo_sqlite answers bindColumn(3, $out) as true/'b' (the true 3rd column's own value) from the full 4-column arity, which our wire's last-wins collapse has already discarded. Alias duplicate columns distinctly instead.

dup.classtype.why: FETCH_CLASS | FETCH_CLASSTYPE reads the class name from the FIRST column positionally (M1 review round 2, R1); when that column's own name is duplicated, this shim now refuses rather than risk answering from a value the wire's last-wins collapse may have silently substituted. Measured: real pdo_sqlite genuinely hydrates an App\Pdo\Fixtures\Row instance from the first occurrence's value, with the object's own `classname` property left holding the SECOND occurrence's value ('bogus-classname') because property hydration collapses duplicate names the ordinary last-wins way, independent of the classtype resolution that reads column 0 positionally — refused_by_us records that ours declines to guess which occurrence a real driver would have honoured in general, rather than relying on this seed happening to name a resolvable class.

dup.fetch_column_index_1.why: fetchColumn(1) over duplicate column names now throws (M1 review F-1, FIX: fetchColumn() reached the wire directly and skipped the same duplicate-column guard every other FETCH_COLUMN path uses, silently answering an unrecoverable collapsed value under duplicates). Real pdo_sqlite answers the SECOND COLUMN's (a.i) own original value — an ordinary int, 1 — from the true 4-value arity (measured); our wire's last-wins collapse has already discarded it before PHP could see it (M1 review round 2, R10: this note previously said 'second occurrence', which is imprecise — index 1 is unambiguously the second column regardless of naming). Alias duplicate columns distinctly (see dup.aliased, which matches) instead.

dup.fetch_column_method.why: fetchColumn() with the default index (0) over duplicate column names now throws (M1 review F-1, FIX: fetchColumn() reached the wire directly and skipped the same duplicate-column guard every other FETCH_COLUMN path uses, silently answering column 0's collapsed value under duplicates). Real pdo_sqlite answers the FIRST occurrence's original value from the true 4-value arity (measured); our wire's last-wins collapse has already discarded it before PHP could see it. Alias duplicate columns distinctly (see dup.aliased, which matches) instead.

dup.fetch_func.why: FETCH_FUNC calls the given callable with EVERY column as a positional arg (`...array_values($row)`); under duplicate column names the collapsed row has fewer entries than the true arity, so the callable would receive too few (and wrong) values (M1 review round 2, R1). Measured: real pdo_sqlite calls the callback with all 4 columns' true values from the full arity, which our wire's last-wins collapse has already discarded before this fetch mode could see them. Alias duplicate columns distinctly instead.

dup.group_assoc.why: FETCH_GROUP/FETCH_UNIQUE key every group by the FIRST column's value, taken positionally, for EVERY base mode they combine with — not only NUM/BOTH/COLUMN, so this refusal is now unconditional on any duplicate rather than scoped to those three (M1 review round 2, R1, a strengthening over the prior narrower guard). Measured: real pdo_sqlite keys the group by the first column's TRUE original value ('a'), which our wire's last-wins collapse has already discarded before this fetch mode could see it. Alias duplicate columns distinctly instead.

dup.key_pair.why: FETCH_KEY_PAIR pairs a row's first value with its second, positionally; two DISTINCT columns sharing a name still pass the 'exactly 2 columns' arity check, but the wire's last-wins collapse folds them into ONE entry, leaving nothing to pair (M1 review round 2, R1). Measured: real pdo_sqlite answers the true 2-value pair {'a': 'b'} (first column's value keyed to the second's) from the uncollapsed row, which our side can no longer recover. Alias duplicate columns distinctly instead.

dup.named.why: FETCH_NAMED groups duplicate columns into an array on real pdo_sqlite (measured); the values that would need grouping are already gone from our wire (the `{column: value}` collapse is last-wins, before PHP ever sees the row), so Branch A's `columns` list (design §2.7) lets this be detected and refused precisely rather than answered wrong. FETCH_NAMED itself IS filled for the no-duplicate case (design §3 F-6) — see the unique-column cases in the Fetch modes group, which match.

dup.num.why: FETCH_NUM over duplicate column names needs the full 4-value arity; our wire already collapsed the row to a 2-key map before PHP saw it (last-column-wins). Branch A's `columns` list (cursor.columnNames, design §2.7) now lets AtomsStatement detect that precisely and refuse loudly instead of silently answering with the wrong arity (the pre-fill deviation) — real pdo_sqlite answers with all 4 original values (measured). Alias duplicate columns distinctly (see dup.aliased, which matches) rather than relying on positional FETCH_NUM over ambiguous column names.

err.not_null_violation.why: A NOT NULL violation throws on both sides with the SAME SQLSTATE 23000 (measured), driver codes differ (1 vs 19) but that is not part of the strict comparison. A genuine refused_by_both, not a gap.

err.syntax_error.why: A SQL syntax error throws on both sides with the SAME SQLSTATE HY000 and the SAME driver code 1 (measured — real pdo_sqlite's own SQLITE_ERROR code); messages differ (sqlite's own wording, never compared) but the SQLSTATE and driver code coincide exactly. A genuine refused_by_both, not a gap.

err.unique_violation.sqlstate.why: A UNIQUE violation throws on both sides with the SAME SQLSTATE 23000 (measured); the driver error codes differ (ours reports 1, real reports 19 — SQLite's own constraint-specific error code, which our bridge does not carry across the wire) but driver code is not part of the strict comparison. A genuine refused_by_both, not a gap.

fetch.bound.unknown_column.why: bindColumn('nope', ...) throws PDOException on both sides for an unknown column name: real pdo_sqlite (measured HY000, "Did not find column name 'nope' in the defined columns; it will not be bound") and ours (design §3 F-2, resolved against Branch A's `columns` list — HY000, same message shape). Both refuse; a genuine refused_by_both, not a gap — bindColumn() by name and by index against a known column IS filled and matches (see fetch.bound.default_type/fetch.bound.param_int).

fetch.classtype.why: FETCH_CLASS | FETCH_CLASSTYPE is FILLED (design §3 F-4) and correctly falls back to stdClass when the data-supplied class name does not resolve (measured directly against the in-guest comparator), matching real pdo_sqlite exactly for THIS case's own classname column. The one remaining difference is the SAME already-pinned root cause as value.float_integral: row 'b's REAL column (r=2.0) round-trips as PHP int(2) on our side, float(2) on real's, because our wire's encodeInt64Deep() cannot distinguish a whole-number REAL from an INTEGER once workerd hands both to JS as the same `number` type. Not a new limitation — an existing one now reachable through a newly-filled path.

fetch.column.out_of_range.why: fetchColumn(5) on a one-column result now throws \ValueError('Invalid column index') on our side (design §3 F-21, FILLED — matches real's exact exception family, measured); real pdo_sqlite throws the SAME family for the same reason. A genuine refused_by_both — an exception pair can never classify as 'match' under this harness's taxonomy even when the behaviour is now identical, since match is reserved for two answered values.

fetch.func.via_fetch.why: fetch(FETCH_FUNC) (not fetchAll()) now throws \ValueError('Can only use PDO::FETCH_FUNC in PDOStatement::fetchAll()') on our side — the SAME family AND wording real pdo_sqlite throws (design §3 F-7, FILLED). A genuine refused_by_both: FETCH_FUNC itself IS implemented (fetchAll(FETCH_FUNC, $callback) matches), this pair is real PDO's own restriction that FETCH_FUNC is fetchAll()-only, correctly reproduced rather than merely refused with the wrong family.

fetch.key_pair.three_columns.why: fetchAll(FETCH_KEY_PAIR) over three columns now throws (design §3 F-26, FIX): real pdo_sqlite requires EXACTLY two columns and throws PDOException HY000 (measured); ours now checks `count($this->columns)` (Branch A) and throws the same family with a real errorInfo triple + getCode() as the SQLSTATE (design §3 F-28's pattern). A genuine refused_by_both, not a gap — FETCH_KEY_PAIR over exactly two columns IS filled and matches (see fetch.key_pair).

fetch.lazy.why: fetch(FETCH_LAZY) throws unconditionally and permanently: real pdo_sqlite returns a PDORow, an internal class bound to a live statement that userland code cannot construct, so there is nothing on our side to reproduce it with (design §3 F-18, mandated to stay throwing).

fetch.ori_abs.why: Same root cause and same permanent posture as fetch.ori_prior (design §3 F-9).

fetch.ori_first.why: Same root cause and same permanent posture as fetch.ori_prior (design §3 F-9).

fetch.ori_last.why: Same root cause and same permanent posture as fetch.ori_prior (design §3 F-9).

fetch.ori_prior.why: fetch() with any orientation other than FETCH_ORI_NEXT throws unconditionally and PERMANENTLY: real pdo_sqlite has no scrollable cursor and, measured, silently IGNORES the orientation and returns the NEXT row regardless — implementing scrolling over our buffer would either diverge from the driver or claim a capability the comparator itself does not have (design §3 F-9, the decisive measurement). Refusing is strictly more honest than the driver's own silent wrong-row behaviour.

fetch.ori_rel.why: Same root cause and same permanent posture as fetch.ori_prior (design §3 F-9).

fetch.set_fetch_mode.class.why: setFetchMode(FETCH_CLASS, Row::class) then fetchAll() is FILLED (design §3 F-17) and hydrates all three rows correctly. The one remaining difference is the SAME already-pinned root cause as value.float_integral: row 'b's REAL column (r=2.0) round-trips as PHP int(2) on our side, float(2) on real's, because our wire's encodeInt64Deep() cannot distinguish a whole-number REAL from an INTEGER once workerd hands both to JS as the same `number` type. Not a new limitation — an existing one now reachable through a newly-filled path.

int.wide.direct_read.why: Reading a stored >2^53-1 INTEGER directly (no CAST) throws a typed int64_precision PDOException on our side: workerd hands ctx.storage.sql INTEGER columns to JS as doubles, so the exact value is already lost before any Atoms code runs (mvp-spec.md Appendix item 1). Real pdo_sqlite reads it exactly. Select the column as CAST(col AS TEXT) instead — see int.wide.cast_read and int.wide.write_exact, which both match.

int.wide.negative_direct_read.why: M1 review F-11: the NEGATIVE end of the wide-int band was previously unexercised. Reading a stored PHP_INT_MIN directly (no CAST) throws the SAME typed int64_precision PDOException as int.wide.direct_read, for the same reason and by the same mechanism, just below zero instead of above 2^53-1 (mvp-spec.md Appendix item 1). Real pdo_sqlite reads it exactly. Select the column as CAST(col AS TEXT) instead — see int.wide.negative_cast_read and int.wide.negative_write_exact, which both match.

pdo.attr.autocommit.why: Both sides refuse getAttribute(ATTR_AUTOCOMMIT): real pdo_sqlite answers SQLSTATE[IM001] (measured) and ours throws AtomsNotSupported. Refused_by_both, matching the driver's own posture exactly.

pdo.attr.client_version.why: getAttribute(ATTR_CLIENT_VERSION) is refused permanently for the same reason as ATTR_SERVER_VERSION: there is no client library on this side of the wire whose version would be truthful to report (design §3 F-22).

pdo.attr.emulate_prepares.why: Both sides refuse getAttribute(ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES): real pdo_sqlite answers SQLSTATE[IM001] (measured) and ours throws AtomsNotSupported. Refused_by_both, matching the driver's own posture exactly.

pdo.attr.server_version.why: getAttribute(ATTR_SERVER_VERSION) is refused permanently: the guest's SQLite build and the Durable Object's SQLite build are two different binaries, so any single answer would misrepresent one of them (design §3 F-22).

pdo.attr.timeout.why: Both sides refuse getAttribute(ATTR_TIMEOUT): real pdo_sqlite itself answers SQLSTATE[IM001] (measured) and ours throws AtomsNotSupported — a genuine refused_by_both, not merely a gap on our side. No fix needed; the driver we claim to be doesn't answer this either.

pdo.prepare.driver_options.cursor_scroll.why: prepare() throws for ANY non-empty $options array; real pdo_sqlite returns false for CURSOR_SCROLL (sqlite has no scrollable cursor). Refusing loudly is honest; use no driver options and PDO::FETCH_ORI_NEXT only.

pdo.prepare.driver_options.statement_cla.why: prepare() throws for ANY non-empty $options array; real pdo_sqlite accepts ATTR_STATEMENT_CLASS. We always return an AtomsStatement regardless, so accepting the option would be a silent lie about the returned class.

pdo.prepare.driver_options.timeout.why: prepare() throws for ANY non-empty $options array today; real pdo_sqlite silently accepts and ignores ATTR_TIMEOUT (measured). There is no driver-owned statement handle for an option to configure, so accepting-and-ignoring would be a silent lie about what the option did.

pdo.query.class_args.why: query() with FETCH_CLASS + a class name + constructor args is FILLED (design §3 F-14, forwards to setFetchMode() then execute()) and hydrates App\Pdo\Fixtures\Row objects correctly. The one remaining difference is the SAME already-pinned root cause as value.float_integral: row 'b's REAL column (r=2.0) round-trips as PHP int(2) on our side, float(2) on real's, because our wire's encodeInt64Deep() cannot distinguish a whole-number REAL from an INTEGER once workerd hands both to JS as the same `number` type. Not a new limitation — an existing one now reachable through a newly-filled path.

pdo.quote.nul_byte.why: quote("a\0b") now THROWS a \PDOException on our side (design §3 F-24's rewrite: quote() always quotes and ignores $type, EXCEPT this one case); real pdo_sqlite silently TRUNCATES the value at the NUL byte and returns "'a'" (measured). This is a deliberate posture, not a gap: silently truncating a value is the one thing this surface must not do, so ours refuses loudly rather than reproducing the truncation — encode NUL-bearing data (e.g. base64) before quoting it.

pdo.quote.param_bool.why: M1 review F-5 (RECLASSIFIED): AtomsPDO::quote() now declares the SAME parameter type real \PDO::quote() does (`string $string, int $type = PARAM_STR`). Under Cases.php's declare(strict_types=1), passing the raw PHP bool `true` for that `string $string` parameter throws \TypeError at the argument boundary on BOTH sides now — real's before its own $type-ignoring quote logic ever runs, ours before its always-quote body ever runs. Same mechanism, same family, on both sides: a genuine refused_by_both, not a comparator-only quirk. Coerce to string yourself (e.g. `$b ? '1' : '0'`) before calling quote() if you need a boolean quoted.

pdo.quote.param_null.why: M1 review F-5 (RECLASSIFIED): same mechanism as pdo.quote.param_bool. AtomsPDO::quote() now declares `string $string` like real \PDO::quote() does, so passing the raw PHP `null` for it throws \TypeError at the argument boundary on BOTH sides under Cases.php's declare(strict_types=1) — a genuine refused_by_both. Coerce to an empty string yourself before calling quote() if you need a NULL-standing-in-for-empty value quoted.

pdo.quote.weak_null.why: Under WEAK typing (no declare(strict_types=1) — CasesWeak.php is the one case file without it, M1 review round 2, R5), quote(null) throws a \TypeError on our side: AtomsPDO::quote()'s own `string $string` parameter (M1 review round 1, F-5) is a USERLAND signature, and userland functions never got PHP's legacy internal-function leniency for passing null to a non-nullable scalar parameter. Real (internal/C) \PDO::quote() still coerces null to the empty string under weak typing (deprecated as of 8.1, but not an error) and returns "''". A userland-vs-internal-function typing gap, not a bridge limitation — pass an explicit '' instead of null.

pdo.setattr.case_upper.why: M1 review F-17 (stale why fixed to describe the CURRENT code): ATTR_CASE IS implemented (design §3 F-22) — setAttribute(ATTR_CASE, CASE_NATURAL) succeeds — but CASE_UPPER/CASE_LOWER are refused with AtomsNotSupported because column-name case folding on fetch is not implemented; fetched keys are always the query's own case. Real pdo_sqlite accepts CASE_UPPER and reshapes subsequent fetch() keys to upper-case, hence refused_by_us. This is a deliberate, permanent restriction, not an unfilled gap.

pdo.setattr.errmode_silent.why: setAttribute(ATTR_ERRMODE, ...) accepts only ERRMODE_EXCEPTION today; the bridge reports every failure by throwing, so ERRMODE_SILENT/WARNING cannot be honoured. Real pdo_sqlite accepts the switch (though nothing on our side could implement silent/warning modes truthfully).

pdo.setattr.stringify_fetches.why: setAttribute(ATTR_STRINGIFY_FETCHES, ...) is not implemented at all today; real pdo_sqlite accepts it. Not yet filled.

stmt.get_attribute.why: Both sides refuse PDOStatement::getAttribute() with the SAME SQLSTATE now (design §3 F-23: AtomsNotSupported's third constructor arg carries 'IM001', matching real pdo_sqlite's measured SQLSTATE[IM001] exactly — there is no driver-owned statement handle to read from on either side). A tightened implementation, not a loosened comparison — refused_by_both with a matching triple, not merely a matching family.

stmt.get_column_meta.why: getColumnMeta() throws unconditionally and PERMANENTLY: real pdo_sqlite answers name/native_type/pdo_type/flags/table/len/precision, and even under this baseline's wire we would only ever have the column NAME — the rest would have to be invented outright (design §3 F-19).

stmt.next_rowset.why: Both sides refuse nextRowset() with the SAME SQLSTATE now (design §3 F-23): real pdo_sqlite itself throws SQLSTATE[IM001] ("driver does not support multiple rowsets", measured) and ours throws AtomsNotSupported constructed with 'IM001' for the same reason (a single result set per statement) — a tightened implementation, refused_by_both with a matching triple.

stmt.set_attribute.why: Both sides refuse PDOStatement::setAttribute() with the SAME SQLSTATE now, for the same reason as getAttribute(): real answers SQLSTATE[IM001] (measured) and ours throws AtomsNotSupported constructed with 'IM001' (design §3 F-23) — refused_by_both with a matching triple, not merely a matching family.

stmt.sqlite_create_aggregate.why: Same permanent reasoning as stmt.sqlite_create_function — an aggregate callback is equally unreachable from the Durable Object's SQL engine (design §3 F-32).

stmt.sqlite_create_collation.why: Same permanent reasoning as stmt.sqlite_create_function — a collation callback is equally unreachable from the Durable Object's SQL engine (design §3 F-32).

stmt.sqlite_create_function.why: sqliteCreateFunction() throws unconditionally and PERMANENTLY: statements execute in the Durable Object, not in the guest, so a PHP callback registered here could never actually be invoked by the engine running the SQL (design §3 F-32). Real pdo_sqlite (same process as the SQL engine) supports it natively.

tx.commit_without_begin.why: commit() with no open transaction throws on both sides — a genuine refused_by_both, both a bare PDOException with no SQLSTATE captured by either driver for this condition on this build.

tx.nested_begin.why: A second beginTransaction() while one is already open throws on both sides (design-expected refused_by_both): ours raises a plain PDOException with no SQLSTATE set, real raises one with no SQLSTATE either on this build — messages differ (never compared) but both are unmistakably "already an active transaction" errors.

tx.rollback_without_begin.why: rollBack() with no open transaction throws on both sides — a genuine refused_by_both, both a bare PDOException with no SQLSTATE captured by either driver for this condition on this build.

value.float_integral.why: A REAL literal holding a whole number (2.0) round-trips as PHP int(2) on our side (typeof still correctly reports 'real' — the storage class is not lost, only the PHP-level type PDO hands back); real pdo_sqlite returns float(2). Root cause: JSON has no int/float distinction for a whole-number token, and our wire's encodeInt64Deep() emits an integral JS number as a plain JSON numeral indistinguishable from an int, so json_decode() on this side always resolves it to PHP int. There is no workaround short of a schema-aware encoder change; do not rely on a computed REAL that happens to be whole staying a PHP float.
